definition: An option is a derivative contract giving its buyer the right, but not the obligation, to buy (call) or sell (put) an underlying asset at a fixed price at a future date, in exchange for an up-front premium.
core_idea: Unlike futures, forwards, and swaps, an option buyer can choose not to exercise, which caps the buyer's downside at the premium paid while preserving upside participation.
key_points: A call option is the right to buy; a put option is the right to sell.
The premium is paid up front by the buyer when purchasing the option, and can be expensive.
For the option buyer, risk is limited to losing the premium; otherwise the buyer profits.

As a rule of thumb, option buyers frequently lose small amounts (the premium) but occasionally realize large profits; option sellers earn a steady stream of small premiums but face occasional large losses — the payout profiles are mirror images of each other.
relationships: Options differ from futures/forwards/swaps specifically in that exercise is optional for the buyer, changing the risk/reward shape versus a fixed obligation.
trading_implications: Buying options is a way to set a worst-case price for an asset while retaining upside, at the cost of the premium; selling options generates regular premium income but exposes the seller to potentially large tail losses.
caveats: Confusing an option's limited-loss profile for the buyer with the seller's risk profile — the seller does not have the same limited downside.
